certainty_reasoning: Legal marriage, documented in the source: Wilde's wedding invitation to Milner with the editors' transcription of the admission card (St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, 29 May 1884), Constance's own engagement letter of 26 November 1883, her honeymoon letters from Paris, and the editorial apparatus on the marriage. Two sons (Cyril, Vyvyan) attested in letters and plate captions read so far.

start.label: engagement announced by Constance, 26 November 1883 (acquaintance from June 1881)

phases.note: Acquaintance and courtship: first met London, June 1881 ('I can't help liking him' - Constance to Otho, 7 June 1881, quoted p. 221 n. 1).
Engagement (Dublin, announced 26 Nov 1883) to wedding (St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, 29 May 1884, 2.30 p.m.).

Marriage: honeymoon Paris (Hotel Wagram, June 1884); two sons; passionate letter of 16 Dec 1884; by 1893 much apart (Constance in Rome/with the boys while Wilde at Babbacombe, p. 555) - but only three letters to her survive, the rest destroyed after her death (p. 241 n. 6).

Trials and separation: hand-delivered notes Feb/April 1895; she visited Reading 19 Feb 1896 to break Lady Wilde's death - their last meeting; changed her and the children's name to Holland and refused Wilde access to the sons (custody/divorce-question pages not yet transcribed - pointer); died Genoa 7 April 1898.

summary: Wilde's wife. Constance Mary Lloyd (1858–1898), daughter of Horace Lloyd QC, met Wilde in London in June 1881, accepted him in Dublin in November 1883, and married him at St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, on 29 May 1884. Two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Only three of Wilde's letters to her survive - a passionate one of December 1884 and two pencilled notes from the 1895 catastrophe; the rest were destroyed after her death. She visited him in Reading Gaol on 19 February 1896 to tell him of his mother's death - their last meeting - kept his allowance, took the name Holland, withheld the children, and died at Genoa on 7 April 1898; Wilde telegraphed 'Am in great grief' and visited her grave in 1899.

sources.quote: My dearest Otho, Prepare yourself for an astounding piece of news! I am engaged to Oscar Wilde and perfectly and insanely happy.
sources.context: Constance Lloyd to her brother Otho Holland Lloyd, 26 November 1883, 1 Ely Place, Dublin. Editors' n. 1 at p. 221 gives her main particulars: "Constance Mary Lloyd (1858–98) was the daughter of Horace Lloyd, QC (1828–74)", and that she "had first met Wilde in London two years earlier" (her letter of 7 June 1881 quoted there).
sources.supports: Engagement 26 November 1883, in Constance's own voice; her dates and parentage from the same page-opening's editorial note.

sources.quote: I am going to be married to a beautiful young girl called Constance Lloyd, a grave, slight, violet-eyed little Artemis, with great coils of heavy brown hair which make her flower-like head droop like a flower, and wonderful ivory hands which draw music from the piano so sweet that the birds stop singing to listen to her. We are to be married in April.
sources.context: Wilde to Lillie Langtry, circa 22 January 1884, Royal Victoria Hotel, Sheffield - announcing the engagement
sources.supports: Wilde's own description of Constance during the engagement; the emotional register of the courtship in his voice.

sources.quote: My dear Milner, I am going to be married tomorrow – quite privately – but would be so glad to see you at the church and afterwards at 100 Lancaster Gate. Enclosed ticket.
sources.context: Wilde to Alfred Milner, [28 May 1884], [London]. Editors' n. 2: "The printed card reads: 'Admit to St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, Thursday, May 29 1884 at 2.30 p.m.'"
sources.supports: Marriage 29 May 1884, St James's Church, Sussex Gardens.

sources.quote: Dear and Beloved, Here am I, and you at the Antipodes. O execrable facts, that keep our lips from kissing, though our souls are one. … I feel your fingers in my hair, and your cheek brushing mine. The air is full of the music of your voice, my soul and body seem no longer mine, but mingled in some exquisite ecstasy with yours. I feel incomplete without you.
sources.context: Wilde to Constance Wilde, Tuesday [Postmark 16 December 1884], The Balmoral, Edinburgh, while on a lecture tour seven months after the wedding. Editors' n. 6: "Except for the brief notes on pp.633 and 637, this is the only letter from Wilde to his wife which is known to have survived. The rest were almost certainly destroyed by her family or her executors after her death."
sources.supports: Passionate marital intimacy in 1884; the destruction of the correspondence (why the record is thin is itself documented).
sources.provenance: repo PDF pp. 263-4 (printed pp. 241-2, folios checked), read as page images 2026-08-03

sources.quote: Dear Constance, Allow no one to enter my bedroom or sittingroom – except servants – today. See no one but your friends. Ever yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Constance Wilde, [? 5 April 1895] — hand-delivered to 16 Tite Street; editors' n. 1 places it "the morning of the last day of the Queensberry trial, when Wilde knew he could not win". The other pencilled note (p. 633, read so far) concerns keeping Cyril away from town in February 1895.
sources.supports: Contact at the catastrophe; the last surviving words from Wilde to his wife.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 689 (printed p. 637, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: I feel that I have brought such unhappiness on her and such ruin on my children that I have no right to go against her wishes in anything. She was gentle and good to me here, when she came to see me. I have full trust in her.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 10 March 1896, HM Prison, Reading, on the marriage settlement. Editors' n. 4: "Lady Wilde had died on 3 February 1896 and Constance travelled specially from Genoa to Reading to break the news to him. Her visit was on 19 February. It was their last meeting." — the note quotes Constance to her brother: "I went to Reading on Wednesday and saw poor O, … he is an absolute wreck compared with what he was."
sources.supports: Her prison visit of 19 February 1896 (their last meeting) and Wilde's deference to her in the settlement.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 703 (printed p. 652, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: Constance is dead. Please come tomorrow and stay at my hotel. Am in great grief. OSCAR
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Robert Ross, [Postmark 12 April 1898], Paris. Editors' n. 1: "Constance Wilde died at Genoa on 7 April 1898, aged forty, and was buried in the Protestant cemetery there." Plate caption 82 (plate section, read so far): Wilde visited the grave a year after her death.
sources.supports: Her death, 7 April 1898, Genoa; Wilde's reaction.

sources.quote: My children are taken from me by an order of the court. I am legally no longer their father. I have no right to speak to them. If I try to communicate with them I can be put into prison for contempt of court. My wife also is of course wounded with me for what she considers a breach of faith on my part. On Monday I sign here a deed of separation of the most painfully stringent kind and of the most humiliating conditions. If I try to communicate with my wife against her will, or without her leave, I lose my wretched £150 a year at once. My life is to be ruled after a pattern of respectability.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 13 May [1897], HM Prison, Reading - written days before release, describing the deed of separation he was about to sign.
sources.supports: Formal separation-in-practice after 1895: custody, allowance conditions, name change, denied access - pages not yet transcribed (Wilde's own 'Constance has not asked me to come and see the children. I don't suppose now I shall ever see them', to Blacker, 6 Sept 1897, p. 935, IS transcribed in the dossier).
